Aim and objectives

Aim. To apply diagnostic test statistics to clinical decisions, moving from pre-test to post-test probability and choosing cut-offs.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Calculate sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and predictive values from a 2×2 table and explain SnNout and SpPin.
  2. Convert pre-test probability to odds, apply a likelihood ratio, and convert post-test odds back to probability.
  3. Explain how moving a cut-off trades sensitivity against specificity on a ROC curve.
  4. Compare tests using area under the ROC curve and identify the optimal cut-off point.
  5. Complete all 30 worked challenges, scoring at least 24 (80%), before you open the working.
  6. Turn all 50 flashcards and mark at least 40 as 'Got it' by the end of today's session.

13.5.2Sensitivity, specificity and accuracy

Big idea. Sensitivity and specificity describe the test, not the patient: each is read down one column of the 2 x 2 table, among people whose true status is already known.
Picture it as a smoke alarm and a nightclub bouncer.

Syllabus: Sensitivity (13.5.2) and specificity (13.5.3), with overall accuracy

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 79 · Sensitivity and specificity →

The story in plain words. A kitchen smoke alarm is built never to miss a fire, so it also shrieks at burnt toast. A nightclub bouncer is built never to let the wrong person in, so now and then he turns away someone who should have been admitted. The alarm is sensitive; the bouncer is specific. Every diagnostic test sits somewhere between the two. Draw the 2 x 2 table with the truth in the columns and the test in the rows. Sensitivity is a / (a + c): of everyone who really has the disorder, the share the test catches. Specificity is d / (b + d): of everyone who is well, the share the test clears. In the diagram, 85 / 100 gives a sensitivity of 85% and 360 / 400 a specificity of 90%. Two partners travel with them. The false negative rate is 1 minus sensitivity and the false positive rate is 1 minus specificity; each pair shares a denominator, so each pair adds up to 100%. Accuracy is (a + d) / N, the share of everyone classified correctly. ((? Why is accuracy a poor single summary? ?)) Because a test that calls everyone well looks highly accurate whenever the disorder is rare.

The diagnostic 2 x 2 table read two ways. Columns hold the truth, rows hold the test result. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. The words were borrowed into medicine by Jacob Yerushalmy, a statistician reading chest X-rays for tuberculosis in the 1940s, and Altman and Bland's short BMJ series of 1994 is still the clearest account. Their point is simple: both measures are calculated within groups of known status, so they belong to the test. Wilson and Jungner's screening principles (1968) add the clinical reason this matters. A screen looks for disease among people who feel well, so missing cases is the costly error, and a screening tool is chosen for high sensitivity, with a second, specific test to confirm.

From everyday life to the clinic. Combining tests moves the balance. In serial testing a person must be positive on both tests, so false positives fall away and specificity rises, while every miss from either stage is kept and sensitivity falls. In parallel testing a positive on either test counts, so sensitivity rises and specificity falls. On a ward this decides how you read results. A highly sensitive test that is negative helps rule out (SnNout); a highly specific test that is positive helps rule in (SpPin). For a woman on a teratogenic drug, two independent negative pregnancy tests each miss with probability 1 minus sensitivity, so the chance both miss is that number squared.

A smoke alarm is built never to miss a fire, so it also sounds for burnt toast (sensitive); a door steward is built never to admit a gatecrasher, so the odd real guest is turned away (specific). Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The commonest slip is the wrong denominator. Sensitivity and specificity divide by the column totals, the people of known status. Dividing by the row totals gives predictive values, a different quantity answering a different question. Watch for tables printed the other way round, with truth in the rows. Rebuild the table in your own layout before calculating. And remember that when two tests share the same specificity, the one with higher sensitivity finds more true cases, whatever the prevalence.

The denominator trap: sensitivity and specificity are read down the columns, among people of known status. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309: 102.
  2. Youden WJ (1950). Index for rating diagnostic tests. Cancer, 3: 32-35.
  3. Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

13.5.4Predictive values and prevalence

Big idea. Predictive values answer the patient's question, what does my result mean, and they change with prevalence even when the test itself does not.
Picture it as the same fishing net cast in a crowded pond and in an almost empty lake.

Syllabus: Predictive values (13.5.4), with prevalence (13.5.1)

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 85 · Predictive values and prevalence →

The story in plain words. Cast the same net into a pond full of trout and almost everything in it is trout. Cast it into a lake with three trout and the net comes up mostly weed. The net has not changed; the water has. That is positive predictive value. PPV is a / (a + b), read across the positive row: of everyone who tests positive, the share who truly have the disorder. Negative predictive value is d / (c + d), the share of negatives who are truly well. These are the numbers a patient cares about, because they start from the result in the patient's hand. The diagram holds the test fixed at 90% sensitivity and specificity and moves it between rooms. At a prevalence of 1% the PPV is only 8%; at 10% it is 50%; at 50% it is 90%. ((? What happens to NPV as prevalence rises? ?)) It falls, because more of the negatives are now missed cases.

Positive and negative predictive value against prevalence for one test with sensitivity and specificity of 90%. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Altman and Bland's second BMJ note (1994) made this the lesson most doctors remember from their series: predictive values cannot be carried from one setting to another without adjusting for prevalence. Leeflang and colleagues (2009) added a refinement. Sensitivity and specificity are not perfectly fixed either, because the mix of mild and severe cases changes between settings. But the large, predictable swing belongs to the predictive values.

From everyday life to the clinic. A depression questionnaire gives a higher PPV in a liaison clinic than in a community survey because depression is commoner among hospital patients. Nothing is wrong with the questionnaire. The same logic explains why a reassuring screen in an older adult with mild memory worries carries real weight: a normal result in a low-prevalence group has a high NPV. It also explains why a diagnostic accuracy study cannot tell you the prevalence in the nation. Its sample was chosen for the study, often enriched with cases, so its prevalence describes the sample, not the population.

One net (catches 90% of fish and 10% of weed) cast in two waters: the share of fish in the catch, the PPV, follows how many fish were there. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Expect a question in which the same test behaves differently in two clinics. The answer is prevalence, not a change in sensitivity or specificity. Expect also a table from a test-evaluation study followed by a question about national prevalence. The answer is that it cannot be estimated from those data. And when asked which measure to quote to a patient holding a negative result, choose the NPV.

Predictive value traps and the correct readings. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.
  2. Lijmer JG, Mol BW, Heisterkamp S, et al. (1999). Empirical evidence of design-related bias in studies of diagnostic tests. JAMA, 282: 1061-1066.
  3. Cohen J (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educ Psychol Meas, 20: 37-46.

13.5.5Likelihood ratios and the Fagan nomogram

Big idea. A likelihood ratio says how much a particular result should shift your belief, and because it is built from sensitivity and specificity it travels between settings.
Picture it as an exchange rate that converts what you believed before into what you should believe now.

Syllabus: Likelihood ratios and nomograms

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 90 · Likelihood ratios and Fagan nomogram →

The story in plain words. An exchange rate turns pounds into euros without caring how many pounds you hold. A likelihood ratio does the same for evidence: it turns pre-test odds into post-test odds, whatever the starting point. The positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity / (1 minus specificity): how many times more likely a positive result is in someone with the disorder than in someone without it. The negative likelihood ratio is (1 minus sensitivity) / specificity. An LR of 1 changes nothing. An LR+ above 10 or an LR- below 0.1 usually changes management. The Fagan nomogram does the arithmetic with a ruler. Mark the pre-test probability on the left, the likelihood ratio in the middle, and read the post-test probability where the straight line meets the right-hand scale. ((? With sensitivity 80% and specificity 90%, what is LR+? ?)) 0.8 / 0.1 = 8.

Fagan nomogram. Starting at a pre-test probability of 10%, a positive result with LR+ 20 moves the probability to 69%; a negative result with LR- 0.1 moves it to 1.1%. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Terrence Fagan published his nomogram as a one-page letter in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1975, so that clinicians could apply Bayes' theorem at the bedside without a calculator. Jaeschke, Guyatt and Sackett's Users' Guide (1994) made likelihood ratios the preferred currency of diagnostic evidence, and Deeks and Altman's BMJ note (2004) explains why: unlike predictive values, likelihood ratios do not depend on prevalence.

From everyday life to the clinic. A gambling-harm screen positive in someone attending an addictions clinic, or a speech-analysis algorithm positive in a research volunteer, can be judged the same way: find the LR, apply it to that person's pre-test odds. Likelihood ratios also work for results with more than two levels, so a very high score can carry a larger LR than a borderline one. That is information a simple positive or negative label throws away.

Likelihood ratios work like exchange rates: the same rate applies whatever you bring. Starting odds 1 to 4 (20%). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The exam likes to offer sensitivity / specificity as a distractor for LR+. The denominator is the false positive rate, 1 minus specificity. It also likes the null value. A likelihood ratio of 1 is useless; zero is not the null. And likelihood ratios describe diagnostic tests, so they are not used as effect sizes in a meta-analysis of treatment trials, where risk ratios, odds ratios and mean differences belong.

Likelihood ratio traps and the correct readings. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes's theorem. N Engl J Med, 293: 257.
  2. Gigerenzer G, Hoffrage U (1995). How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats. Psychol Rev, 102: 684-704.
  3. Leeflang MMG, Bossuyt PMM, Irwig L (2009). Diagnostic test accuracy may vary with prevalence: implications for evidence-based diagnosis. J Clin Epidemiol, 62: 5-12.
  4. Streiner DL, Norman GR, Cairney J (2015). Health Measurement Scales: A Practical Guide to Their Development and Use, 5th ed. Oxford University Press.

13.5.6Pre-test and post-test probability

Big idea. Diagnosis is updating: start with how likely the disorder was before the test, convert to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio, then convert back.
Picture it as a weather forecast revised after you look out of the window.

Syllabus: Pre-test odds, post-test odds and probabilities

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 90 · Likelihood ratios and Fagan nomogram →

The story in plain words. The morning forecast says a 20% chance of rain. You look out and see black clouds, and you revise upwards. You did not start from nothing and you did not jump to certainty. That is how a test result should be used. The forecast is the pre-test probability, which in a study equals the prevalence in the people tested. Turn it into odds: p / (1 minus p), so 20% becomes 1 to 4. Multiply by the likelihood ratio to get the post-test odds, then convert back with odds / (1 + odds). The tree in the diagram does the same sum with people instead of formulae. Of 1000 referrals, 100 have dementia and 80 of them test positive; of the 900 without, 90 test positive anyway. Only 80 / 170, about 47%, of positives truly have dementia. ((? Pre-test 10%, LR+ 9: post-test probability? ?)) Odds 1/9 x 9 = 1, so the probability is 0.5.

Natural frequency tree for 1000 referrals with prevalence 10%, sensitivity 80% and specificity 90%: 80 of the 170 positives truly have dementia. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. The engine is Bayes' theorem, published after Thomas Bayes's death in 1763. In odds form it is short enough to carry in your head: post-test odds equal pre-test odds times the likelihood ratio. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) showed that students who fail the formula often solve the same problem easily when it is told as natural frequencies, so many people out of 1000. The tree is not a simplification; it is the better way to think.

From everyday life to the clinic. A woman referred to a memory clinic where one in four has dementia, with a positive cognitive test of sensitivity 80% and specificity 80%, has LR+ 4. Pre-test odds of 1/3 become 4/3, a probability of about 0.57. So even a reasonable test leaves her only a little more likely than not to have dementia. That is a conversation about uncertainty and further assessment, not a diagnosis delivered on one score.

A forecast of 20% rain (odds 1 to 4) revised after seeing clouds four times more likely before rain: odds 1, a 50% chance. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The classic error is multiplying a probability, not the odds, by the likelihood ratio. A pre-test probability of 0.3 times an LR of 5 gives 1.5, which cannot be a probability. The second is forgetting the starting point. Sensitivity is not the chance that a positive patient has the disease, and a post-test probability can stay modest when the pre-test probability was low.

Post-test probability traps; the worked numbers differ from those in the questions. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.
  2. Bland JM, Altman DG (1986). Statistical methods for assessing agreement between two methods of clinical measurement. Lancet, 327: 307-310.
  3. Streiner DL, Norman GR, Cairney J (2015). Health Measurement Scales: A Practical Guide to Their Development and Use, 5th ed. Oxford University Press.

13.5.7Cut-offs, ROC curves and the area under the curve

Big idea. Where two groups' scores overlap, every cut-off trades sensitivity against specificity; the ROC curve draws all those trades at once and its area says how well the scores separate the groups.
Picture it as a dimmer switch sliding between two overlapping crowds.

Syllabus: Receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) and AUC

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 96 · ROC curves, AUC and cut-off →

The story in plain words. Picture two crowds on a field, one well and one unwell, standing at their screen scores. They overlap in the middle. Wherever you draw the line, some unwell people stand on the well side and some well people on the unwell side. Sliding the line is like turning a dimmer switch: brighter for one error, darker for the other. Lower the cut-off and more people are positive: sensitivity rises, specificity falls and false positives multiply. Raise it and the opposite happens. When a disease is deadly but curable if caught early and positives can be confirmed cheaply, choose a low cut-off and accept false positives. The ROC curve plots sensitivity against 1 minus specificity for every cut-off. The diagonal is a coin toss, AUC 0.5; a perfect test hugs the top-left corner, AUC 1. The shoulder of the curve, where the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity minus 1) is largest, is the best balanced cut-off. ((? What does the x-axis show? ?)) The false positive rate, 1 minus specificity.

Left: screen scores in people with and without the disorder; the cut-off of 50 leaves false negatives (burgundy) and false positives (grey). Right: the ROC curve traced by sliding the cut-off, with the chance diagonal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. ROC analysis came from radar operators in the Second World War, judging which blips were aircraft. Hanley and McNeil (1982) gave medicine its most useful reading: the AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen person with the disorder scores higher than a randomly chosen person without it. Youden (1950) proposed his index as a single number for a cut-off, and Altman and Bland's third BMJ note (1994) shows how ROC curves compare two tests: the curve nearer the top-left corner is the better test.

From everyday life to the clinic. A gambling-harm screen scored 0 to 4 gives one 2 x 2 table for each cut-off. Count the people at or above the cut-off as positive, cumulatively. A cut-off of 0 calls everyone positive, so sensitivity is 100% and specificity 0%. On a perinatal questionnaire, the cut-off with the highest PPV is the highest one, because only the most certain cases remain positive. The best balanced cut-off is usually in the middle.

An airport scanner dial: each setting is a cut-off, trading blades found against innocent alarms. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Where the exam tries to catch you. An AUC of 0.5 does not mean the test is half as good as the reference standard. It means no discrimination at all. Read cumulative tables carefully: raising a cut-off can lower sensitivity without changing specificity if no unaffected person scored in the band you removed. And on the ROC graph, the point furthest to the right has the lowest specificity.

Cut-off and ROC traps and the correct readings. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J, et al. (eds) (2023). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.4. Cochrane.
  2. Bayes T (1763). An essay towards solving a problem in the doctrine of chances. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 53: 370-418.

Layout of the validation study: screen result against the reference-standard assessment of delirium. Illustrative teaching figure drawn for CDA.
A brief delirium screen on a medical ward is validated against a reference-standard assessment, laid out as in the table. Which expression gives the overall accuracy of the screen?
  1. True positives / everyone with delirium
  2. (True positives + true negatives) / everyone tested
  3. True negatives / everyone without delirium
  4. True positives / everyone who screens positive
  5. Everyone with delirium / everyone tested
Show the working
Answer: B (True positives + true negatives) / everyone tested

Accuracy pools both kinds of correct result over the whole sample. It is a blunt summary because it shifts with prevalence and hides the balance between false positives and false negatives, which is why sensitivity and specificity are reported separately.

Rule: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / N.
Trap: Confusing accuracy with sensitivity.
Delirium presentDelirium absent
Screen positivea True positiveb False positive
Screen negativec False negatived True negative
Accuracy = (a + d) / (a + b + c + d): the correct diagonal over everyone tested
top of the fraction rest of the denominator
Accuracy uses all four cells. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Challenge 2 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.2
The two-stage memory pathway described in the question. Illustrative teaching figure drawn for CDA.
A memory service uses two tests in series, as shown in the pathway: everyone receives a brief cognitive screen, and only those who screen positive go on to a longer neuropsychological battery. A person is called a case only if positive on both. Compared with either test used alone, this two-stage strategy will have
  1. Higher sensitivity and lower specificity
  2. Higher sensitivity and higher specificity
  3. Unchanged sensitivity and specificity
  4. Higher specificity and lower sensitivity
  5. Properties that depend on the prevalence of dementia
Show the working
Answer: D Higher specificity and lower sensitivity

A person must clear two hurdles to be labelled a case, so fewer healthy people are wrongly labelled, but any case missed by either stage is lost. Serial testing suits situations where false positives are costly and the second test is expensive.

Rule: Serial (both positive) raises specificity; parallel (either positive) raises sensitivity.
Trap: Mixing up serial and parallel testing.
Serial testing worked through with counts. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Celentano DD, Szklo M (2019). Gordis Epidemiology, 6th ed. Elsevier.

A new 20-item questionnaire for adult ADHD is tested against a specialist diagnosis; the results are shown in the table. What are its specificity and false positive rate?
  1. 80% and 20%
  2. 67% and 20%
  3. 80% and 33%
  4. 57% and 43%
  5. 20% and 80%
Show the working
Answer: A 80% and 20%

Specificity and the false positive rate share the same denominator (everyone without the condition) and always add up to 100%. The same applies to sensitivity and the false negative rate.

Working: true negatives = 300 minus 60 = 240; specificity 240/300 = 80%; false positive rate = 1 minus specificity = 20%.

Rule: False positive rate = FP / all non-diseased = 1 minus specificity.
Trap: Using all test positives as the denominator for the false positive rate.

Answer: E 8

Sensitivity 0.8, specificity 0.9, so false positive rate 0.1; 0.8 / 0.1 = 8. A likelihood ratio of this size produces a moderate to large shift in probability.

Working: LR+ = (40/50) / (5/50) = 0.8 / 0.1 = 8.

Rule: LR+ = Sn / (1 minus Sp).
Trap: Dividing by specificity instead of 1 minus specificity.

Challenge 9 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.7
Weekly alcohol intake in people with and without hazardous drinking, with the current and proposed screening thresholds. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A pilot screening programme defines hazardous drinking as more than 21 units a week. The figure shows the proposal to lower the threshold to more than 14 units. Which change is most likely?
  1. Fewer true positives
  2. Lower sensitivity
  3. Fewer false positives
  4. Higher positive predictive value
  5. More false positives
Show the working
Answer: E More false positives

Moving the cut-off trades false negatives for false positives. A lenient threshold catches more cases at the cost of mislabelling more people; a strict threshold does the opposite.

Rule: Lower threshold: Sn up, Sp down, more FPs.
Trap: Assuming a lower cut-off improves every property.
Computed from the curves shown in the question. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Using the table of questionnaire performance, at which cut-off does a woman who screens positive have the highest probability of truly having perinatal depression?
  1. >2
  2. >10
  3. >4
  4. >6
  5. >8

Answer: B >10

Raising the cut-off removes false positives faster than true positives, so PPV rises, though sensitivity falls sharply. The best cut-off depends on the purpose of testing.

Rule: Highest probability after a positive = highest PPV.
Trap: Picking the cut-off with the best sensitivity.
The table plotted. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Calling everyone positive guarantees no false negatives but makes the test useless. The question illustrates the extreme end of the trade-off.

Rule: The lowest cut-off maximises sensitivity.

Challenge 13 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.7
ROC curve of a new self-rated anxiety screen against a diagnostic interview. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A new self-rated anxiety screen is plotted as a ROC curve against a diagnostic interview (shown), with an area under the curve of 0.50. This means the screen
  1. Is half as good as the interview
  2. Has 50% sensitivity at every cut-off
  3. Discriminates no better than chance
  4. Discriminates moderately well
  5. Discriminates very well
Show the working
Answer: C Discriminates no better than chance

AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen person with the condition scores higher than a randomly chosen person without it. At 0.5 the scores overlap completely.

Rule: AUC: 0.5 chance, 1.0 perfect.
Trap: Reading AUC as a percentage of the gold standard.
Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

Challenge 14 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.7
Accuracy of a self-rated anxiety screen at cut-off scores 2 to 8 against a diagnostic interview; dashed line is the diagonal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What is the graph shown called?
  1. Forest plot
  2. Funnel plot
  3. Galbraith plot
  4. Receiver operating characteristic curve
  5. Kaplan-Meier curve
Show the working
Answer: D Receiver operating characteristic curve

ROC curves are used to choose cut-offs and to compare tests: the curve nearer the top-left corner, with the larger area beneath it, discriminates better.

Rule: Sensitivity versus 1 minus specificity = ROC.
Trap: Confusing it with the other named plots.
Anatomy of a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve: sensitivity against 1 minus specificity, one point per cut-off. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Challenge 15 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.7
Accuracy of a self-rated anxiety screen at cut-off scores 2 to 8 against a diagnostic interview; dashed line is the diagonal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the ROC graph shown, what does the dashed diagonal line represent?
  1. A test that does not discriminate between people with and without the disorder
  2. The best possible test
  3. The reference standard interview
  4. A test with moderate discrimination
  5. The median survival curve
Show the working
Answer: A A test that does not discriminate between people with and without the disorder

Any point on the diagonal is no better than guessing in proportion. The area under the diagonal is 0.5.

Rule: Diagonal = chance; top-left corner = perfect.
Trap: Thinking the diagonal is a target to reach.
When the disorder makes no difference to the score, every cut-off catches the same share of both groups, so sensitivity equals the false positive rate and the points fall on the diagonal (area 0.5). Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

Challenge 16 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.7
Accuracy of a self-rated anxiety screen at cut-off scores 2 to 8 against a diagnostic interview; dashed line is the diagonal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
On the x-axis of the ROC graph, 1 minus specificity represents the
  1. True positive rate
  2. False positive rate
  3. False negative rate
  4. True negative rate
  5. Accuracy
Show the working
Answer: B False positive rate

Because specificity and the false positive rate share a denominator, they always sum to 100%. Moving right on the x-axis means more false alarms.

Rule: 1 minus Sp = FPR.
Trap: Reading the x-axis as specificity.
Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Two index tests (a brief structured screening interview and a blood marker) applied to the same 400 liaison-psychiatry referrals, against a reference-standard clinical diagnosis. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the table, how does the blood marker compare with the structured interview?
  1. Lower sensitivity and higher specificity
  2. Higher sensitivity and higher specificity
  3. Higher sensitivity and lower specificity
  4. Lower sensitivity and lower specificity
  5. Same sensitivity and specificity
Show the working
Answer: C Higher sensitivity and lower specificity

Read down the columns by true status: of 250 with the disorder, the marker detects 225 and the interview 200; of 150 without, the marker clears 105 and the interview 135. The marker catches more cases but mislabels more healthy people.

Working: marker sensitivity 225/250 = 90% versus 200/250 = 80%; marker specificity 105/150 = 70% versus 135/150 = 90%.

Rule: Sensitivity = TP / all diseased; specificity = TN / all non-diseased.
Trap: Dividing by the row totals (test results) instead of the true-status totals.
Sensitivity (of 250 with the disorder)Specificity (of 150 without)
Screening interview200 / 250 = 80%135 / 150 = 90%
Blood marker225 / 250 = 90%105 / 150 = 70%
Marker: more cases caught, more healthy people mislabelled
Each property is read down its own column of true status. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Challenge 18 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.2
Probability tree for repeat urine pregnancy tests in a woman who is pregnant. Illustrative teaching figure drawn for CDA.
A woman on an acute ward who is prescribed a teratogenic mood stabiliser may be pregnant. A urine pregnancy test with sensitivity 95% and specificity 98% is negative, and a repeat test the next day is also negative. Using the probability tree for a woman who is in fact pregnant, with the two results independent, what is the probability of two negative results?
  1. 1 in 20
  2. 1 in 50
  3. 1 in 400
  4. 1 in 2500
  5. 19 in 20
Show the working
Answer: C 1 in 400

In a pregnant woman each test is falsely negative with probability 0.05. For two independent tests the probabilities multiply.

In practice repeat tests are not fully independent, so the true risk is somewhat higher.

Working: the false negative rate is 1 minus 0.95 = 0.05, and 0.05 x 0.05 = 0.0025 = 1/400.

Rule: P(negative | disease) = 1 minus sensitivity; multiply for independent repeats.
Trap: Using specificity, which describes people without the condition.
Probability tree for a woman who is pregnant. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Celentano DD, Szklo M (2019). Gordis Epidemiology, 6th ed. Elsevier.

Distribution of scores on a four-item gambling-harm screen in 120 addiction-clinic attenders, against a clinician diagnosis. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the gambling-harm screen data in the table, what can be said about the prevalence of gambling disorder in the UK adult population?
  1. About 33%
  2. About 13%
  3. About 22%
  4. It cannot be estimated from these data
  5. About 3%
Show the working
Answer: D It cannot be estimated from these data

Diagnostic accuracy studies recruit people suspected of the condition, so the sample proportion reflects referral patterns. Population prevalence requires a representative sampling frame.

Rule: Prevalence needs a representative sample of the population.
Trap: Reading the sample proportion as national prevalence.
Why a test-evaluation sample cannot give population prevalence. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Celentano DD, Szklo M (2019). Gordis Epidemiology, 6th ed. Elsevier.

Challenge 20 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.6
Blank Fagan nomogram. Draw a line from the pre-test probability through the likelihood ratio to read the post-test probability, or calculate with odds. Illustrative teaching tool drawn for CDA.
An 80-year-old man attends a memory clinic where 20% of men his age referred from primary care prove to have dementia. He scores below the cut-off on a test with sensitivity 90% and specificity 80%. Using the Fagan nomogram or calculation, what is the probability that he has dementia?
  1. 0.20
  2. 0.80
  3. 0.53
  4. 0.90
  5. 0.18
Show the working
Answer: C 0.53

Convert probability to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio, then convert back. Because dementia is fairly uncommon in this group, even a reasonable test leaves the probability only around one in two.

Working: LR+ = 0.9/0.2 = 4.5; pre-test odds = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25; post-test odds = 1.125; probability = 1.125/2.125 = 0.53.

Rule: Post-test odds = pre-test odds x LR; probability = odds / (1 + odds).
Trap: Multiplying the pre-test probability (not the odds) by the LR.
The odds route for this patient. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Deeks JJ, Altman DG (2004). Diagnostic tests 4: likelihood ratios. BMJ, 329: 168-169.

Challenge 21 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.6
Blank Fagan nomogram. Draw a line from the pre-test probability through the likelihood ratio to read the post-test probability, or calculate with odds. Illustrative teaching tool drawn for CDA.
Audit data suggest that one in five people referred to a perinatal team has an anxiety disorder. A questionnaire with sensitivity 90% and specificity 85% is positive in a new referral. Using the Fagan nomogram or calculation, her probability of having an anxiety disorder is closest to
  1. 0.20
  2. 0.85
  3. 0.60
  4. 0.90
  5. 0.75
Show the working
Answer: C 0.60

Odds = p / (1 minus p), so a one in five probability is odds of 1 to 4. Multiply by the LR of 6 to get 1.5, then probability = 1.5 / 2.5.

Working: LR+ = 0.9/0.15 = 6; pre-test odds = 1/4; post-test odds = 1.5; probability = 1.5/2.5 = 0.60.

Rule: Probability 1 in 5 = odds 1 to 4.
Trap: Treating 1 in 5 as odds of 1/5.
The odds route for this referral. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes's theorem. N Engl J Med, 293: 257.

Challenge 22 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.7
Biomarker levels in people with and without a rare, rapidly fatal neurological disease; positive if at or above the cut-off. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A cheap biomarker is being considered to screen for a rare, rapidly fatal neurological disease that is curable if treated early; positives can be confirmed with a definitive test. Using the figure, which cut-off is most appropriate?
  1. A
  2. C
  3. B
  4. D
  5. E
Show the working
Answer: C B

When missing a case is catastrophic and false positives can be cleared by a confirmatory test, choose the cut-off that maximises sensitivity, but no lower than needed, because each further step adds false positives without benefit.

Rule: Fatal, treatable, confirmable: set the cut-off to avoid false negatives.
Trap: Choosing the most specific cut-off because the disease is rare.
Computed from the curves shown in the question. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Wilson JMG, Jungner G (1968). Principles and Practice of Screening for Disease. Public Health Papers 34. Geneva: World Health Organization.

Trap: Reading 100% NPV as meaning a positive is certain.

Distribution of scores on a four-item gambling-harm screen in 120 addiction-clinic attenders, against a clinician diagnosis. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Using the gambling-harm screen table, which cut-off gives the best overall balance of sensitivity and specificity, judged by the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity minus 1)?
  1. 1 or more
  2. 2 or more
  3. 4 only
  4. 3 or more
  5. 0 or more
Show the working
Answer: D 3 or more

Calculate sensitivity and specificity cumulatively at each cut-off, then compare J. Where specificity is already 100%, the positive likelihood ratio becomes infinite, which is why J or the ROC curve is a better guide to balance.

Working: Youden: 1 or more = 0.40; 2 or more = 0.63; 3 or more = 0.65; 4 = 0.40.

Rule: Youden J = Sn + Sp minus 1; the maximum marks the ROC point furthest above the diagonal.
Trap: Choosing the middle cut-off by habit without calculating.
Computed from the score table. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Youden WJ (1950). Index for rating diagnostic tests. Cancer, 3: 32-35.

Challenge 26 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.7
Accuracy of a self-rated anxiety screen at cut-off scores 2 to 8 against a diagnostic interview; dashed line is the diagonal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the ROC graph, which numbered cut-off offers the best trade-off between sensitivity and specificity?
  1. 2
  2. 4
  3. 6
  4. 8
  5. 5
Show the working
Answer: E 5

At the shoulder, further gains in one property cost a disproportionate loss in the other. The point also has the largest Youden index here.

Rule: Best balance = elbow of the curve, nearest the top-left corner.
Trap: Picking the highest sensitivity point.
Computed from the ROC points in the question. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Youden WJ (1950). Index for rating diagnostic tests. Cancer, 3: 32-35.

Challenge 27 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.2
Two blood tests for a rare metabolic cause of psychosis are compared in 300 patients. Test X has sensitivity 85% and specificity 95%. Test Y has sensitivity 93% and specificity 95%. Which statement is correct?
  1. Test X will correctly identify more of the patients who have the condition
  2. Test Y will correctly identify more of the patients who do not have the condition
  3. The prevalence is needed to say which test finds more true cases
  4. Neither test will produce any false positives
  5. Test Y will correctly identify more of the patients who have the condition
Show the working
Answer: E Test Y will correctly identify more of the patients who have the condition

Sensitivity is the proportion of diseased people who test positive. If both tests are applied to the same group, the test with the higher sensitivity will detect more of the true cases, regardless of how many cases there are.

Rule: Same specificity: the higher sensitivity wins on true positives.
Trap: Thinking prevalence is needed; it changes the absolute numbers, not which test finds more.
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Challenge 28 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.2
A commissioner must choose a questionnaire to screen for depression in people attending diabetes clinics, with positives referred for a full assessment. Which single property should weigh most in favour of a questionnaire for this purpose?
  1. Specificity of 65%
  2. Positive predictive value of 15%
  3. Available in several languages
  4. Sensitivity of 90%
  5. Takes two minutes to complete
Show the working
Answer: D Sensitivity of 90%

A screen is a first filter. A highly sensitive screen means a negative result reliably rules the condition out (SnNout), while the false positives it generates are dealt with by the confirmatory assessment.

Rule: Screening: prioritise sensitivity; confirm with a specific second step.
Trap: Choosing brevity or language versions over the core job of finding cases.
Why a screen favours sensitivity: the second step removes false positives, nothing recovers a miss. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Wilson JMG, Jungner G (1968). Principles and Practice of Screening for Disease. Public Health Papers 34. Geneva: World Health Organization.

Challenge 29 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.4
A 78-year-old retired librarian worried about her memory scores well within the normal range on a cognitive screen performed by the GP. Which property of the screen best tells the GP how far this normal result reassures her that she does not have dementia?
  1. Negative predictive value
  2. Sensitivity
  3. Specificity
  4. Positive predictive value
  5. Inter-rater reliability
Show the working
Answer: A Negative predictive value

Sensitivity and specificity condition on true disease status, which the clinician does not know. Predictive values condition on the test result, which the clinician does know, so they answer the patient's question.

They depend on the prevalence in the population tested.

Rule: Positive result: think PPV. Negative result: think NPV.
Trap: Choosing sensitivity because a highly sensitive test rules out (SnNout); the question asks what this result means for her.
DementiaNo dementia
Screen abnormala True positiveb False positive
Screen normalc False negatived True negative
Her result sits in the bottom row. NPV = d / (c + d)
top of the fraction rest of the denominator
A normal result is read across the negative row. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309: 102.

Challenge 30 · 13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.4
The same depression questionnaire is used under identical conditions in a community survey and in a general hospital liaison clinic. A positive result is much more likely to indicate true depression in the liaison clinic. The most likely explanation is
  1. Depression is more prevalent among liaison clinic patients
  2. The questionnaire is more specific in the community
  3. The questionnaire is less sensitive in the liaison clinic
  4. Depression is more prevalent in the community
  5. The cause cannot be judged without repeating the survey
Show the working
Answer: A Depression is more prevalent among liaison clinic patients

With a fixed test, more true cases in the tested population means a greater share of positives are true positives. This is why a test validated in a specialist setting gives a much lower PPV when it is used for screening in the community.

Rule: Higher prevalence: PPV up, NPV down.
Trap: Assuming sensitivity and specificity changed between settings.
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309: 102.

Part 3 · 50 flashcards

Tap a card to turn it. Each card is one concept. Answer it out loud, then turn it: the answer, why, what to remember, the trap and why the other options are wrong.

CARD 1
13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.4
As the prevalence of a condition in the population screened increases, which property of the screening test increases?
D) Positive predictive value

Remember. Prevalence up: PPV up, NPV down.

Trap. Choosing NPV.

Why not the others.
A) Sensitivity: A property of the test, conditional on disease.
B) Specificity: A property of the test, conditional on no disease.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 2
13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.5
Which expression gives how many times more likely a positive test result is in a person with the disorder than in a person without it?
D) Sensitivity / (1 minus specificity)

Remember. LR+ = Sn / (1 minus Sp); LR minus = (1 minus Sn) / Sp.

Trap. Swapping the formulae for LR+ and LR minus.

Why not the others.
A) (1 minus sensitivity) / specificity: This is the negative likelihood ratio.
B) Sensitivity / specificity: Not a standard measure.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 3
13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.5
Which property of a diagnostic test is, in principle, not altered by the prevalence of the condition in the population tested?
A) Positive likelihood ratio

Remember. Sn, Sp and LRs travel; predictive values do not.

Trap. Treating predictive values as fixed properties of a test.

Why not the others.
B) Positive predictive value: Rises with prevalence.
C) Negative predictive value: Falls with prevalence.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 4
13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.6
In a study evaluating a diagnostic test, the prevalence of the condition in the population studied corresponds to which quantity?
B) Pre-test probability

Remember. Prevalence = pre-test probability.

Trap. Confusing pre-test probability with pre-test odds.

Why not the others.
A) Post-test probability: The probability after the result.
C) Pre-test odds: Derived from prevalence but expressed as odds.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 5
13.12 Appraising diagnostic and screening studies · 13.5.5

A meta-analysis pools randomised trials of a psychological intervention for panic disorder.

Which of the following would NOT normally be used to express the pooled treatment effect?
  1. Risk ratio
  2. Likelihood ratio
  3. Odds ratio
  4. Standardised mean difference
  5. Mean difference
B) Likelihood ratio

Remember. Intervention effect sizes: RR, OR, RD, MD, SMD; not likelihood ratios.

Trap. Thinking any ratio can be an effect size.

Why not the others.
A) Risk ratio: Commonly pooled for binary outcomes.
C) Odds ratio: Commonly pooled for binary outcomes.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 6
Test propertyValue
Sensitivity90%
Specificity70%
Properties of a diagnostic test
13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.5

A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 70%. The table shows the test's properties.

What is the positive likelihood ratio?
D) 3.0

Remember. LR plus = sensitivity / (1 minus specificity). (LR plus = hit rate over false-alarm rate)

Trap. Dividing sensitivity by specificity.

Why not the others.
A) 0.14: 0.14 is the negative LR (0.1 / 0.7).
B) 0.43: 0.43 is (1 minus specificity) divided by specificity, 0.3 / 0.7, the wrong way up.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 7
13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.5
Which likelihood ratio means that the test result makes no difference to the probability of disease?
C) 1

Remember. LR = 1 is useless. LR plus over 10 or LR minus under 0.1 is strong. (One means nothing learned)

Trap. Thinking an LR of 0 is the null value.

Why not the others.
A) 0: An LR of 0 would mean the result never occurs in disease.
B) 0.5: 0.5 halves the odds of disease.

✓ Got it↻ Again
CARD 8
13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.5
A test with very high sensitivity is most useful for
B) Ruling out a diagnosis when negative

Remember. SnNout: sensitive test, negative result, rules out. SpPin: specific test, positive result, rules in. (SnNout and SpPin)

Trap. Reversing the mnemonics.

Why not the others.
A) Confirming a diagnosis when positive: Ruling in needs high specificity.
C) Estimating prevalence: Prevalence is a population measure.

✓ Got it↻ Again

13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.5

A new dementia screen is positive in 90 of 100 patients with dementia and negative in 85 of 100 cognitively intact controls. The table shows these results.

Which statement is correct?
  1. Sensitivity 85%, specificity 90%
  2. Sensitivity 90%, specificity 85%
  3. PPV 90%
  4. NPV 85%
  5. False-positive rate 10%
B) Sensitivity 90%, specificity 85%

Remember. Sensitivity from the cases, specificity from the controls. (Cases give sensitivity, controls give specificity)

Trap. Reporting the false-positive rate as 10%.

Why not the others.
A) Sensitivity 85%, specificity 90%: The figures are reversed.
C) PPV 90%: PPV depends on prevalence and here equals 90 / 105 = 86%.

  4. Negative predictive value is the proportion of test-negative people who are truly free of the condition
  5. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition whom the test detects
C) A test that is highly sensitive is, for that reason, usually highly specific as well
